bib.title: Chain-of-Agents: End-to-End Agent Foundation Models via Multi-Agent Distillation and Agentic RL

legacy_report: SOURCE: "Chain-of-Agents: End-to-End Agent Foundation Models via Multi-Agent Distillation and Agentic RL", OPPO AI Agent Team (Weizhen Li, Jianbo Lin, and others; corresponding author Wangchunshu Zhou). arXiv:2508.13167. The page-1 stamp reads v1, 6 Aug 2025, and the Date line says August 20, 2025. Preprint, 2025. COVERAGE: I read all 51 pages (201,541 chars extracted), from the abstract through the conclusion, the contributions page, the appendix headings and the Appendix B results. I skimmed or skipped three things. - References (pp. 23-27): skimmed for origins only. - Appendix C case-study trajectories and Appendix D prompts (pp. ~29-51): read headings only. - Figures 1, 5 and 6: the numbers are garbled in extraction. The `figures.py captions` script returned nothing. CLAIMS (ranked) - claim: AFM-RL 32B (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct base) beats the previous best tool-integrated-reasoning (TIR) math results. It scores 59.8 on AIME25 against ReTool-32B at 49.3, and averages 78.0 against ReTool-32B at 74.4. number: 59.8 AIME25; 78.0 avg; +10.5 AIME25; +5.7 OlympiadBench setup: Table 11; 32B; avg@16 for AIME24, AIME25 and AMC23; pass@1 for MATH500 and OlympiadBench. Math-Verify scoring. Code-agent model. quote: "At the 32B scale, AFM-RL-32B attained an average accuracy of 78.0%, which is 3.6% higher than the current state-of-the-art ReTool-32B. Notably, on the datasets AIME25 and OlympiadBench, AFM-RL-32B achieved absolute improvements of 10.5% and 5.7% respectively" where: p. 16 and Table 11, p. 17 - claim: RL adds a large gain on top of SFT. For the code agent, SFT accounts for roughly half the improvement over the backbone and RL for the rest (7B and 32B). At 32B the SFT model scores 60.0 on average and RL lifts it to 78.0. number: 7B: SFT +22.0, RL +20.8; 32B: SFT +23.4, RL +18 setup: Table 11 averages. Base 21.5 → 43.5 → 64.3 at 7B; 36.6 → 60.0 → 78.0 at 32B. The paper reports percentage-point differences. quote: "For the 7B model, SFT contributed an average accuracy gain of 22.0%, with RL providing an additional 20.8% improvement over the SFT baseline. For the 32B model, the corresponding gains are 23.4% from SFT and 18% from RL." where: p. 16 - claim: On web agents, AFM-RL 32B (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) reaches new highs among 32B models. number: GAIA 55.3, WebWalker 63.0, BrowseComp 11.1 (Table 7) or 11.0 (Table 13), HLE 18.0 setup: Pass@1, Table 7. Compared with WebSailor 53.2 on GAIA, WebShaper 51.4 on WebWalker, and WebThinker-RL 15.8 on HLE (QwQ-32B backbone). Text-only subsets: GAIA 103 items, HLE 500. The LLM judge is Qwen2.5-72B, which also serves as the reward judge in training. quote: "it achieves a new state-of-the-art (among the same model size) average success rate of 55.3% on the GAIA benchmark. This represents a significant 2.1% improvement over WebSailor" where: p. 13, Table 7 p. 12. Table 8 gives the SFT-only 32B figures: GAIA 50.5, WebWalker 61.5, BrowseComp 10.0. - claim: Multi-agent distillation alone (SFT) is already competitive. RL adds a smaller but consistent gain on multi-hop QA (MHQA). number: 7B-instruct avg 41.7 (SFT) → 45.5 (RL); 3B-base 39.7 → 41.3; 7B-base 43.0 → 45.2 setup: Table 6, seven QA sets. Trained on NQ and HotpotQA only; evaluated on the others as out-of-domain. quote: "our framework achieves 41.3% (Qwen-2.5-3B-base), 40.8% (Qwen-2.5-3B-instruct), 45.2% (Qwen-2.5-7B-base), and 45.5% (Qwen-2.5-7B-instruct)" where: p. 13, Table 6 p. 11 - claim: Code generation improves with SFT then RL. Code-agent RL gains over the backbone are 8.5 points average at 7B and 13.2 at 32B. number: 32B LiveCodeBench v5: SFT 43.1 → RL 47.9. CodeContests: 22.4 → 32.7. Backbone Qwen2.5-Coder-32B: 28.1 on LCB v5 and 0.6 on CodeContests. setup: Table 12, pass@1. The table has unlabelled duplicate "AFM-SFT/AFM-RL" rows; I read the first pair as 7B and the second as 32B (inferred, not labelled). quote: "RL-refined models gain an additional 1.8% (7B) and 3.2% (32B) over their SFT counterparts" where: p. 16-17, Table 12 - claim: AFM uses fewer tokens and tool calls than multi-agent systems and other TIR agents. number: 84.6% lower token cost versus traditional multi-agent systems (intro claim) setup: Figure 5, 10 randomly sampled GAIA instances, compared with OAgents and WebThinker. Per-successful-task tool calls and tokens. Bar values are garbled in extraction, so 84.6% rests on the intro only. quote: "AFM reduces the inference cost (in terms of token consumption) by 84.6% compared to traditional multi-agent systems while achieving competitive performance." where: p. 3; Section 5.1, p. 17-18 - claim: Pass@3 and best-of-3 lift AFM more than they lift other open agents. number: GAIA 55.3 → 57.3 (Bo3, judged by Qwen2.5-72B) → 69.9 (Pass@3). HLE 18.0 → 23.0 → 33.2. WebWalker 63.0 → 78.7 (Pass@3). setup: Table 13, 32B. Pass@3 counts a task solved if any of 3 attempts is correct, so it is an oracle selector. quote: "On GAIA, it surges to 69.9—representing a remarkable 14.6-point increase over the base AFM (55.3)" where: p. 19-20 - claim: Tool-format generalization is asymmetric. The code-agent model, trained under strict formatting, orchestrates unseen tools (web search, visual inspector) from the prompt alone. The web-agent model fails on character-precise tool formats. number: none (qualitative; no counts given) setup: GAIA test set; tool schemas inserted in the prompt. The code agent was trained only on a Python interpreter. quote: "In the vast majority of test cases, the web-agent model fails to generate invocations that satisfy these fine-grained format constraints, resulting in parser errors and task abortion." where: p. 18-19 - claim (design details): The method has four parts. - SFT data: multi-agent trajectories from OAgents, in a think/plan/tools/observation/reflection/answer format. - Four filters: complexity (<5 interactions dropped), quality, reflection enrichment, error-correction upsampling. - Loss: observation tokens masked. - RL: DAPO (via VeRL) on queries a 72B model without tools solves at r_q <= 0.3 over 32 tries. Code queries solved 8/8 by a 7B AFM are dropped. number: SFT 16,433 web trajectories (8,826 MHQA plus 7,607 web); ~47k code traces in the text, but Table 9 sums to 59,929. RL 169,615 MHQA, 10,427 web, 47,560 code. setup: Web RL: 64 prompts x 8 rollouts, <=24 steps, 32k tokens. Code RL: 8 rollouts, <=8 tool calls, 150 steps at 7B and 120 at 32B, context 16k to 32k at step 40. quote: "Queries with rq > 0.3 are excluded as they either represent: 1) Trivially solvable cases requiring no tool usage, or 2) Highly contaminated samples vulnerable to parametric recall." where: pp. 6-9, 11, 14-16 - claim (reward design): Web reward is binary LLM-as-judge, with no format reward because SFT already fixes format. Code reward is answer correctness times format. quote: "Rweb(τ)= scoreanswer"; "Rcode(τ)= scoreanswer ⋅ scoreformat" where: p. 8-9 - This matches the target note's "SFT first so RL can parse the output" thread. - Cold start by SFT gives format; RL then runs without a format reward. - claim (RL dynamics): During 32B code RL, training reward and response length both rise steadily and AIME25 avg@16 improves. number: none (curves only; the text gives no numbers) where: Figure 7, p. 28 LIMITS - No ablation of "chain-of-agents vs plain ReAct/TIR on the same data". The advantage over TIR baselines is shown, but data and filtering differ across baselines, so the paradigm effect is not isolated. - Teacher-bounded: the SFT data come from OAgents only. - The efficiency claim is based on 10 GAIA instances. - Pass@3 is an oracle and Bo3 relies on a 72B judge. The same family judges both training reward and evaluation for web tasks. - AIME24 and AIME25 have 30 problems each (avg@16 used to reduce variance). - The paper has no limitations section and no discussion of reward hacking, RL compute cost, or failure analysis. The code-agent training set does not deduplicate prompts between the SFT and RL sets, and the authors say they rely on DAPO's filtering. - The paper reports no pass@k-versus-base analysis, so it does not address the "RL re-weights base capability" question in the note. - Text inconsistencies: ~47k code SFT traces in the text against 59,929 in Table 9; BrowseComp 11.1 against 11.0; the text says "WebDancer 51.5 on GAIA", which Table 7 attributes to QwQ-32B; the Table 12 rows are unlabelled; AFM comparisons mix "base" and "instruct" backbones across rows. BUILDS ON - ReAct (Yao et al., [68]) and Tool-Integrated Reasoning: Search-R1 (Jin et al. 2025), WebThinker, WebDancer, WebSailor, WebShaper, ReTool (Feng et al. 2025), SimpleTIR, ToRL. - OAgents (Zhu et al., [82]) as the teacher multi-agent system. - Agentic task generation from Shi et al. [49]. - Sequence-level knowledge distillation (Kim and Rush [24]), extended to agent-level distillation. - DAPO (Yu et al. [69]) via the VeRL framework (Sheng et al. [48]). - LLM-as-judge following [76]. CODE: none. The paper has no code listings. It prints the trajectory format in Eq. 7's description: ` Ccot αm(αp) Ot Ft ... At ` (p. 7). The code-agent format is `\n```py\n...```\n` (p. 9). FIGURES (the script returned no captions, so these are from the extraction) - Figure 2 (p. 5): TIR's static think-action-observation loop beside CoA's flexible mix of role agents (plan, reflect, verify) and tool agents. It is the fastest way to explain the paradigm. - Figure 3 (p. 6): multi-agent distillation converting OAgents runs into trajectories, with a worked `` example. - Figure 4 (p. 7): the pipeline of cold-start SFT with observation masking, then RL on queries with pass rate <0.3. - Figure 5 (p. 18): tool calls and tokens against OAgents and WebThinker. - Figure 7 (p. 28): RL training reward, response length and AIME25 over steps. PROBLEMS - Figures 1, 5 and 6 have garbled axis text and values in the extraction. - No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. - Note check: `/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/05-RL/notes/05-post-training-for-agents.md` does not cite this paper (arXiv:2508.13167). It has no row for it in its sources list, and the note's SFT-then-RL, observation-masking and "form first, spirit second" sections would be the natural place for it.
